About

Research is the foundation of creativity and design.

Kehinde Arojojoye is a User Experience Designer who excels at performing the research necessary to maximize the quality of experience of all users by combining in-depth research with simple design that applies complex details. Kehinde believes that the right design can make users feel seen and understood, bringing them back to the site, and turning a user into a customer.

Kehinde has completed the UI/UX Bootcamp from the University of Maryland Global Campus. Kehinde holds a bachelor's degree for Information Science from UMD College Park.

When he is conducting user research, Kehinde can be found making music and art or playing soccer.

Work / Cortex

Cortex

A premium-subscription flow for a media platform, built so free viewers choose to upgrade instead of getting pushed into it.

01

Description of the Project

The brief was a "Media Company" scenario: design a path that leads both new and returning users toward subscribing to a premium tier. It's a UX problem as much as a UI one, since the interface has to make the upgrade feel earned.

My UX skills were tested through interviews, usability tests, and research into how industry leaders handle the same problem. My UI skills were tested through a style guide and wireframes, refined into a prototype across two rounds of testing.

02

My Role

I was the lead designer on this project, working solo. I owned research, UX, UI, and usability testing end to end, and a design mentor checked in for critique and direction at each phase.

03

My Team

This was an independent project. My "team" was one design mentor, who reviewed my work at each phase and pushed back on soft spots before I moved forward.

04

Problem

Media apps lose free users at the exact moment they're asked to pay, because the free tier hasn't shown them enough value yet. I needed a user flow, for both new and returning viewers, that surfaces the case for Premium naturally inside the product instead of gating it behind a hard paywall.

05

Research

I studied industry leaders YouTube, Spotify, and Pandora, taking notes on how each one navigates users toward its premium tier. There's no single playbook: each company nudges users differently, so I wrote a competitive research paper scoring all three against the factors I thought mattered most.

Competitive research: scoring rubric and a close read of Spotify's premium flow.

06

Concept Sketches

Before any screen was drawn, I sketched the flow by hand, mapping every route a viewer could take from opening the app to hitting a wall that Premium solves, including the sign-in and payment detours.

07

Art Board

The name "Cortex" was chosen to signal intelligence and savviness, and that promise had to show up in the palette and type before a single UI screen existed. The palette leans on a confident green and a cool neutral grey, paired with a display face that has enough personality to carry the brand.

08

Low Fidelity Prototype

Low-fidelity wireframes came next, built in Figma with just enough fidelity to test structure and wording. Keeping it plain meant testers reacted to the flow itself, before that flow was ever validated.

09

Usability Tests

Round one tested the low-fidelity prototype over Zoom against a script built to probe the most important features. The notes showed my wording needed to be clearer. Round two tested a higher-fidelity prototype and asked about visuals too, which pushed the direction toward something more restrained and closer to professional patterns.

10

High Fidelity

The final design carries the Cortex branding through custom art direction and type, in a modern UI language inspired by current trends like Apple's liquid glass. Premium prompts sit inside natural stopping points in the viewing flow rather than blocking the screen outright.

Open in Figma →
11

Insights

01

Free-tier quality signals premium value

Companies invest different amounts in their premium experience, and that shows up in how pleasant the free tier already feels. The upgrade pitch works better when the free version isn't punishing.

02

A name can carry the brand's promise

The product name "Cortex" was chosen deliberately to signal intelligence and savviness, setting the tone for the visual and interaction design before a single screen was drawn.

03

Modern UI trends move fast, and imitate the leaders

Studying pro interfaces on Mobbin, Behance, and Dribbble showed how quickly trends like Apple's "liquid glass" ripple across the industry, and how similar top-tier products end up looking.

＋

Learnings

The real lesson was about visual language more than UX. I understood the flows and the psychology well, but until I broke down reference patterns from professional interfaces line by line, my UI was trying too hard to be original instead of being clear.

Work / Havenly Homes

Havenly Homes

A mobile-first home-buying app built to turn an overwhelming, jargon-heavy process into something a first-time buyer can actually navigate.

01

Description of the Project

The brief: design a prototype for an app that solves a real, specific problem, start to finish. I chose home buying, because so much of the process is opaque to first-time buyers, and shaped it into Havenly Homes.

UX skills were tested through interviews, usability tests, article research, personas, and red routes. UI skills were tested through wireframes and a style guide, refined into a prototype against real usability feedback.

02

My Role

I was the lead designer on this project, working solo. I owned research, UX, UI, and usability testing end to end, and a design mentor checked in for critique and direction at each phase.

03

My Team

This was an independent project. My "team" was one design mentor, who reviewed my work at each phase and pushed back on soft spots before I moved forward.

04

Problem

First-time home buyers face a process that's fragmented across agents, listings, and paperwork, with no single place that explains what to do next. I needed a mobile-first experience that turns that maze into a guided, confidence-building path from "just looking" to "made an offer."

05

Research

Research started with a screener survey to find the right participants, followed by an empathy map to understand what buyers say, do, think, and feel. Those four don't always agree, which is exactly why mapping them separately mattered. Interviews were then compiled into a persona and a set of prioritized user stories.

Screener survey, empathy map, persona, and prioritized user stories.

06

Concept Sketches

Early concepts were sketched by hand first, laying out the homepage and the buy, rent, and sell routes before touching Figma. Settling the structure early meant visual polish only started once the layout actually worked.

07

Art Board

A shared kit of components, including buttons, icons, and other common elements, kept the interface consistent as screens multiplied. A moodboard kept the photography and colour palette aligned throughout. The discipline of minimalism carried straight through, since less thrown at the user is easier for the user to act on.

Component kit and moodboard, the shared visual language for every screen.

08

Low Fidelity Prototype

Wireframes translated the sketches into a testable structure: the tour-scheduling flow, a listing detail screen, and the homepage buy flow. All three were designed mobile-first, since a mobile layout expands cleanly into desktop but the reverse rarely works.

Low-fidelity wireframes: tour scheduling, listing detail, and the homepage buy flow.

09

Usability Tests

With wireframes in hand, I checked the priority tasks from the red routes against the built structure to make sure they stayed reachable in as few taps as possible. It was a quieter form of testing than a moderated session, but it kept scope honest before moving to high fidelity.

10

High Fidelity

Havenly Homes gives first-time buyers a mobile-first path through home search that mirrors the priorities set by the red routes. It's built around minimalism, so the app never throws more information at a buyer than the moment calls for.

11

Insights

01

The persona made needs concrete

Compiling interview data into a single average user turned scattered opinions into a clear list of needs to design against, and a way to differentiate from competitors.

02

Hierarchy matters more than completeness

User stories showed that buyers want a lot of things, but only a few matter first. The rough draft needed to start with those and add detail later.

03

Designer knowledge isn't user knowledge

Because I built the site from the ground up, I understood it perfectly. Users meet it for the first time though, carrying their own biases, so clarity had to be designed in deliberately rather than assumed.

＋

Learnings

Designing from the ground up means I always know how Havenly Homes is supposed to work. Every user meets it cold though, with their own assumptions. My job was making the interface clear and intuitive enough to close that gap. I'd also change how I framed my early research, which chased the housing crisis in general instead of the buying experience specifically.
